document.title: Constellation Energy Generation, LLC submits Limited Request for Rehearing and Clarification of the 06/18/2026 Order

pages.text:
2 
First, the Commission should modify the June 2026 Co-Location Order to require study 
deadlines, which are the most critical path for the speedy interconnection of Co-Located Loads 
and would be logically consistent with the ANOPR Show Cause Order.3 
Second, the Commission should require PJM to spell out in its Tariff the methodology and 
process (including deadlines) for completing Necessary Studies. These terms belong in the Tariff, 
and not the Manuals, because they “significantly affect rates, terms, and conditions” of service and 
are “readily susceptible to specification.”4 
Third, the Commission should modify the operational penalty for the misoperation of 
control technologies and/or protections to include only a two-strike disqualification as opposed to 
a 120-day suspension on top of a two-strike disqualification. A 120-day suspension has no added 
reliability benefit, is inconsistent with existing practice, and could have a chilling effect that could 
result in costly and unnecessary Network Upgrades. 
Fourth, as Constellation recommended, the Commission should mitigate Transmission 
Owners’ proposals that give them unfettered discretion over the timelines and technical 
requirements for necessary control technologies and/or protection systems. The Commission 
should also require all Transmission Owner standards, requirements, guidance, and practices 
related to necessary control technologies and/or protection schemes for Co-Location 
Arrangements to be on file with the Commission.5 The Commission failed to articulate its 
reasoning for rejecting these recommendations, rendering its decision arbitrary and capricious. 
 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 (2026) (“ANOPR Show Cause Order”). 
4 Energy Storage Ass’n v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 162 FERC ¶ 61,296, at P 103 (2018) (citing Cal. Indep. Sys. 
Operator Corp., 122 FERC ¶ 61,271, at P 16 (2008)). 
5 Response Brief of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 et al., at 10-12 (Apr. 24, 2026) 
(“Constellation Apr. 24 Response Brief”).

3 
In addition, Constellation seeks clarification, or in the alternative, rehearing on the 
Commission’s denial of Constellation’s request to modify the definition of Co-Located Load 
Generating Facility so that only the portion of the Generating Facility serving the Co-Located Load 
be considered the Co-Located Generating Facility. When only a portion of a Generating Facility’s 
capacity is dedicated to serving co-located non-network load (say, a 100 MW non-network load is 
co-located with a 500 MW generator), then only that portion should be considered a Co-Located 
Generating Facility and required to delist. Alternatively, Constellation seeks rehearing on this 
issue. Constellation also requests that the Commission clarify the filing of an Interim Network 
Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) application by an applicant with a pending NITS 
application does not restart the NITS process, sending the applicant to the “back of the line.” 
STATEMENT OF ISSUES/SPECIFICATIONS OF ERROR 
In accordance with section 713 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,6 
Constellation respectfully submits the following statement of issues and specifications of error:  
1. The June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because it fails to 
meaningfully address Constellation’s comments that a replacement rate for the new 
transmission services must include study deadlines. The June 2026 Co-Location 
Order is also arbitrary and capricious because its failure to establish study deadlines 
for the new transmission services is inconsistent with the contemporaneously issued 
ANOPR Show Cause Order requiring study deadlines for the provision of 
transmission service for large loads, and the Commission fails to acknowledge this 
inconsistency. Each of these shortcomings renders the June 2026 Co-Location 
Order arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); Motor Vehicle Mfrs. 
Ass’n of U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (“State 
Farm”); New England Power Generators Ass’n v. FERC, 881 F.3d 202, 210-11 
(D.C. Cir. 2018) (“NEPGA”). 
2. The June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because it fails to 
explain why Necessary Studies provisions that determine required upgrades—and 
therefore significantly affect the rates, terms, and conditions of service—may be 
 
6 18 C.F.R. § 385.713(c)(1)-(2).

4 
relegated to unenforceable PJM Manuals rather than included in the Tariff. See 5 
U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43. 
3. The June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because its finding 
that suspending new transmission service for an Eligible Customer up to 120 days 
after the first misoperation of control technologies and/or protection systems is just 
and reasonable is not adequately supported by the facts, is logically inconsistent 
with the Commission’s finding that PJM’s one-strike proposal for failing to follow 
a curtailment or load shed directive is “unnecessarily strict,” and fails to engage 
with Constellation’s arguments that a 120-day suspension is not consistent with 
existing practice. Each of these shortcomings render the June 2026 Co-Location 
Order arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); State Farm, 463 U.S. at 
43; Burlington Truck Lines v. United States, 371 U.S. 156, 168 (1962) 
(“Burlington”); NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 210-11. 
4. The June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because it confers 
unfettered discretion upon the Transmission Owners with respect to necessary 
control technologies and protection systems without consideration of comments 
advising otherwise. Failure to consider comments raised renders the June 2026 Co-
Location Order arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); State Farm, 463 
U.S. at 43; NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 210-11. 
5. If the Commission does not clarify the definition of Co-Located Generating 
Facility, the June 2026 Co-Location Order is arbitrary and capricious because it 
fails to provide a logical basis for denying Constellation’s request that only the 
portion of the Generating Facility serving the Co-Located Load be considered the 
Co-Located Generating Facility. Failure to consider comments raised renders the 
June 2026 Co-Location Order arbitrary and capricious. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); 
State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43; NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 210-11. 
REQUEST FOR REHEARING 
I. 
The Commission Should Require Study Deadlines Binding Both PJM and the 
Transmission Owners. 
The June 2026 Co-Location Order fails to engage with repeated requests for the 
Commission to direct PJM and the Transmission Owners to establish and comply with study 
deadlines for the new transmission services, which are imperative for the speedy interconnection 
of large loads.7 The Commission “decline[d] to direct PJM to provide more detail in its Tariff on 
 
7 See, e.g., Constellation Apr. 24 Response Brief at 2 (“Two simple solutions can prevent discrimination and delay: 
first, deadlines for deliverables from the Transmission Owners, such as studies, and second, requiring standards,

5 
the process for studying requests for Interim NITS”—but did not provide any discussion of study 
deadlines.8 For Firm Contract Demand Service and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, the 
Commission directed that PJM adopt more precise terms and conditions similar to “the cluster 
study process” and study procedures in the Non-Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service,9 
respectively, but also did not require study deadlines. The lack of study deadlines and any mention 
of them is a failure to engage in reasoned decision making and bad policy. 
First, failure to engage with comments raised is a violation of the Administrative Procedure 
Act (“APA”).10 Summarizing comments is not sufficient.11 The Commission must take the next 
step of providing a substantive response to the comments raised. 
Second, the absence of binding and enforceable deadlines for the new transmission services 
is inconsistent with the June 2026 Co-Location Order itself, where the Commission acknowledged 
 
practices, and technical requirements to be clear and on file at the Commission.”); id. at 11 (“the Commission can 
direct PJM to establish deadlines for studies and other Transmission Owner approvals or consultation requirements. 
Deadlines are commonplace in PJM’s Tariff and procedures”); Constellation Energy Generation, LLC Reply Brief, 
Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 et al., at 17-18 (Mar. 25, 2026) (“Constellation Mar. 25 Reply Brief”) (“Deadlines and 
other mechanisms must be set forth in the Tariff to prevent Transmission Owners from needlessly delaying studies 
and unreasonably denying new transmission services.”); id. at 15 (“PJM must spell out in the Tariff the studies that 
it will perform in conjunction with the Co-Located Generating Facility and the timetable for completing these 
studies.”); id. at 23 (“[A] detailed description of the studies to be performed and the timelines they are to be 
completed must be on file as they are a key element of the service to be provided and will directly implicate the time 
to provide such service.”); id. at 9 (“Clarification of what additional studies need to be performed, and the timeline 
for such studies, will streamline the process.”); Protest and Comments of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000, at 17 (Mar. 16, 2026) (“Constellation 60-Day Compliance Filing Comments”) (“To 
achieve speed to market, there must be deadlines set forth in the Tariff to prevent needless and discriminatory 
delays.”). 
8 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 575. 
9 Id. PP 370, 373. 
10 NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 211 (finding “that FERC did not engage in the reasoned decisionmaking required by the 
Administrative Procedure Act” because it “failed to respond to the substantial arguments put forward by Petitioners 
and failed to square its decision with its past precedent”) (emphasis added). 
11 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 366 (“Constellation requests that the Commission deter 
delays and potential disputes by … establishing deadlines for studies and other transmission owner approvals or 
consultation requirements”); id. P 368. (“Constellation contends that the Commission should … direct that … studies 
be on file, including study deadlines.”); id. P 358 (“Vistra and Constellation … argue that PJM provides no timelines 
or deadlines for processing transmission service requests”).

6 
that “PJM also does not address a timeline for its study process,”12 yet declined to direct PJM to 
establish one. The lack of study deadlines is also inconsistent with the Commission’s preliminary 
finding in the contemporaneously issued ANOPR Show Cause Order that PJM’s Tariff is unjust 
and unreasonable because it lacks “a study deadline of no more than 60-90 calendar days” for 
transmission service requests by Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads.13 The June 2026 Co-
Location Order does not acknowledge this inconsistency or attempt to reconcile it. The concerns 
animating the ANOPR Show Cause Order study deadlines are the same as those that parties have 
raised in the PJM Co-Location proceeding. Failure to square precedent is a failure to engage in 
reasoned decision-making.14 
Third, failure to require study deadlines binding on both PJM and the Transmission Owners 
is bad policy. The delays that have plagued the Necessary Study process demonstrate this. The 
absence of binding and enforceable deadlines has allowed Transmission Owners to refuse to 
participate in the Necessary Study process and delay the interconnection of large loads for years.15 
 
12 Id. P 372. 
13 ANOPR Show Cause Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 at P 63. 
14 See NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 211 (finding “that FERC did not engage in the reasoned decisionmaking required by the 
Administrative Procedure Act” because it “failed to respond to the substantial arguments put forward by Petitioners 
and failed to square its decision with its past precedent”) (emphasis added); see also State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43 
(“Normally, an agency rule would be arbitrary and capricious if the agency … offered an explanation for its decision 
that runs counter to the evidence before the agency ….”); id. (“[T]he agency must examine the relevant data and 
articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action including a ‘rational connection between the facts found and the 
choice made.’”) (quoting Burlington, 371 U.S. at 168). 
15 See, e.g., Complaint Requesting Fast Track Processing of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Constellation 
Energy Generation, LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-20-000, at 7 (Nov. 22, 2024) (“Exelon 
is refusing to process necessary studies on these grounds, demanding expensive upgrades under their unfiled 
interconnection procedures, delaying agreed-upon work which will force a nuclear plant to take additional outages, 
and forcing additional services to be procured.”) (“Constellation Complaint”); id. at 7-8. (“Exelon fulfilled its 
responsibilities as an interconnection provider to review PJM’s necessary studies for one Constellation nuclear 
station, the LaSalle Clean Energy Center (‘LaSalle’), but later refused to do so at the other two stations, insisting 
that Constellation or its potential customer must first apply for retail service and designate what sort of wholesale 
transmission service it will take from Exelon.”); id. at 17 (“But for Constellation’s … Limerick Clean Energy Center 
(‘Limerick’) in Pennsylvania, Exelon has refused to conduct its review of PJM’s completed necessary studies,

7 
Deadlines binding only PJM, but not the Transmission Owners, have failed to produce the timely 
completion of studies. Indeed, PJM’s Form of Necessary Studies Agreement provides that PJM’s 
“good faith estimate for the time of completion of Necessary Studies is within 270 days,” or just 
less than 9 months, from the date that PJM “approves the dynamic model and data submitted by 
Project Developer.”16 Yet (and aside from the inconsistency with the 60 to 90 day timing in the 
ANOPR Show Cause Order), Constellation has been waiting years for Necessary Studies for 
multiple projects, where the Transmission Owner simply refused to cooperate with PJM. New 
transmission service requests will be subject to the same delays unless the Commission requires 
PJM to establish and enforce deadlines that bind both PJM and the Transmission Owners. 
 
insisting that Constellation or its potential customer must first apply for retail service and designate what sort of 
wholesale transmission service it will take from Exelon.”); id. at 8 (“projects are being held hostage by a few 
monopolies refusing to cooperate with reliability studies related to interconnection modifications”); id. at 10 n.25 
(“Exelon refuses to review co-location reliability studies as required by the OATT and pro forma ISA”) (citing 
Constellation PDO Protest, Exhibit 1, Declaration of James R. McCoskey at ¶ 13); id. at 16 (“Proposed Fully Isolated 
Co-Located data center projects in PJM are currently being held hostage by one or two monopoly utilities’ refusal 
to cooperate … with reliability studies related to interconnection modifications.”); see also Constellation Energy 
Generation, LLC November 21, 2025 Supporting Comments, Docket No. RM26-4-000, at 3-4 (Nov. 21, 2025) 
(“Some Transmission Owners have simply refused to participate in PJM’s studies to analyze reliability impacts; and 
some, acting under unfiled interconnection study procedures, have changed their entire construct and timetable for 
processing load studies.”); Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. et al., 
Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al., at 3 (Apr. 23, 2025) (“The Indicated Transmission Owners read the existing Tariff 
to require this one-size-fits-all limitation, and they have refused to perform studies for new load seeking a different 
configuration.”); id. at 14 (“What is more, regardless of what the Tariff actually says and does not say, some of the 
Indicated Transmission Owners have refused to cooperate in PJM’s ‘necessary studies’ process unless the load 
agrees to taking NITS, claiming justification under the Tariff. Some of the Indicated Transmission Owners have 
refused to process necessary studies, demanded expensive upgrades under their unfiled interconnection procedures, 
and forced a generator seeking to serve co-located load to procure additional services not required by the Tariff.”) 
(citing Constellation Complaint at 7); Constellation Complaint at 9 (“Exelon’s also is refusing to perform work on 
LaSalle’s interconnection facilities to accommodate co-location, none of which affects the grid. Exelon’s refusal to 
complete previously agreed-upon work as scheduled during an upcoming planned outage will increase costs to 
Constellation by $15.3-$19 million at that site alone, just so Exelon can pursue its litigation positions.”); see also 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, at P 75 (2025) (“[T]here are allegations in the record that Exelon 
has delayed work on Constellation’s requests to co-locate load with its generators at certain facilities due to Exelon’s 
concerns that such requests are not allowed under the Tariff without arranging for wholesale transmission or retail 
distribution service.”). 
16 PJM Tariff, Part IX, Subpart G, § 15 (Form of Necessary Studies Agreement).

8 
Using its authority to establish a just and reasonable replacement rate,17 the Commission 
should modify its June 2026 Co-Location Order to require PJM to establish such study deadlines. 
Requiring PJM to establish a deadline would not constrain PJM’s discretion in determining how 
best to maintain the reliability of the transmission system. PJM would remain free to propose 
appropriate deadlines, provided those deadlines are reasonable. 
The Commission also should require PJM to establish Necessary Study deadlines binding 
both PJM and the Transmission Owners. While the December 2025 Co-Location Order did not 
direct revisions to the Necessary Study process,18 the Commission has the authority to modify its 
orders before the record is filed in the court of appeals.19 Here, the record demonstrates that PJM’s 
Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because the Necessary Studies provisions do not support their 
timely completion.20  
II. 
The Commission Should Direct PJM to Clarify its Necessary Study Process in its Tariff 
Instead of its Manual. 
In response to our argument that PJM’s proposed tariff revisions identifying the scope of 
the Necessary Study Process requires “additional clarity,”21 the Commission “direct[ed] PJM to 
specify in its compliance filing what types of additional detail about the studies will be available 
in the PJM manuals.”22 Additional details should be included in the Tariff, not the Manuals.  
 
17 16 U.S.C. § 824e. 
18 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 281 (“While parties request that the Commission establish 
deadlines for the Necessary Study process, we note the December Order did not include any such requirement, and 
our review of these proposed Tariff revisions is limited to whether PJM complies with the directives in the December 
Order.”). 
19 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a) (“[T]he Commission may at any time, upon reasonable notice and in such manner as it shall 
deem proper, modify or set aside, in whole or in part, any finding or order made or issued by it under the provisions 
of this Act.”). 
20 See supra note 15. 
21 Constellation 60-Day Compliance Filing Comments at 12. 
22 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 280.

9 
Necessary Studies, along with the methodology and process for performing them and the 
results that methodology and process will produce, “significantly affect rates, terms, and 
conditions”23 of generator interconnection. While including high-level descriptors of the “studies” 
to be performed in the Necessary Study Process is an improvement to PJM’s current Tariff,24 PJM 
must also include in the Tariff a description of the methodology and process for performing the 
studies, including deadlines for completing the studies and any consultation requirements. A 
framework for how Necessary Studies will be performed and completed is not a “mere 
implementation detail[]”25 that may remain unenforceable and subject to unilateral change without 
notice or Commission oversight.26 How studies are performed determines whether a planned 
modification will have a “permanent material impact on the Transmission System” and the 
upgrades to the Transmission System that are deemed “necessary.”27 And like the Tariff 
requirements for studies performed for other interconnection and transmission requests,28 a 
 
23 Energy Storage Ass’n v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 162 FERC ¶ 61,296 at P 103. 
24 Id. 
25 See Hecate Energy Greene Cnty. 3 LLC v. FERC, 72 F.4th 1307, 1312 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (“The tariff need not include 
mere implementation details.”). 
26 See RWE Clean Energy, LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 194 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 38 (2026) (“The 
Commission does not review and approve PJM’s manuals, as they are not filed with the Commission. As a result, 
we have no statutory obligation to enforce the terms of Manual 14B.”) (citations omitted). 
27 PJM Tariff, Part VII, Subpart A, § 400 (definition of (“Necessary Study”). 
28 See, e.g., id. Part VI, Attachment D (Methodology for Completion of System Impact Study); TranSource, LLC v. 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 168 FERC ¶ 61,119, at P 83 (2019) (requiring that PJM include in its Tariff “high-
level summaries of: (1) a definition of the models used to evaluate IARR requests, including descriptions of the 
IARR market model and the planning model; (2) a description of how the market limits or operative constraints in 
the market model are determined; and (3) a detailed explanation of how ‘simultaneous feasibility’ is determined for 
IARR requests, including a description of how PJM conducts the ‘simultaneous feasibility test’ and determines the 
‘incremental capability required’ for IARR requests to be granted”); see also ISO New England, Inc., 187 FERC 
¶ 61,017, at P 13 (2024) (“the meter data submission deadline is a key component of metering practices for DER 
Aggregators that should be included in the basic description of metering practices in the Tariff”).

10 
description of the Necessary Studies methodology and process, including study and consultation 
deadlines, is “readily susceptible to specification.”29  
The Necessary Study Process is a leading cause of the delay of co-located load 
interconnections. The Commission should ensure rules on the Necessary Study Process are clearly 
stated in the Tariff, so that everyone – transmission owners and market participants alike – know 
the applicable rules, which can then be enforced by the Commission. 
III. 
A Two-Strike Disqualification Is a Sufficient Deterrent and Alone Should Be the Just 
and Reasonable Replacement Rate. 
The Commission failed to adequately support its finding that suspending new transmission 
service for an Eligible Customer up to 120 days after the first misoperation of control technologies 
and/or protection systems is just and reasonable.30 While an investigation of the misoperation is 
appropriate, imposing a four-month suspension while the investigation is ongoing is not. The 
Commission should reject the 120-day suspension and approve only the two-strike disqualification 
penalty for the misoperation of control technologies and/or protection systems as the just and 
reasonable operational penalty. 
First, suspending service for an Eligible Customer for 120 days will have no added 
deterrence value or reliability benefit on top of imposing a two-strike disqualification penalty.31 A 
two-strike disqualification penalty will sufficiently incentivize Co-Located Loads to make sure 
they are “willing and able to limit their energy withdrawals.”32 Faced with the commercial risk 
 
29 Energy Storage Ass’n v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 162 FERC ¶ 61,296 at P 103. 
30 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 516. 
31 Id. P 524 (“We find that this replacement rate serves to deter conduct contrary to the fundamental principle around 
which the new transmission services created by the Commission were based, i.e., that Eligible Customers taking 
service on behalf of Co-Located Loads are willing and able to limit their energy withdrawals from the transmission 
system under certain conditions.”). 
32 Id. P 524.

11 
(and potential commercial penalties) of disqualification and the years-long NITS process,33 Co-
Located Loads will seek to ensure they do not cause or allow the misoperation of necessary control 
technologies and/or protections schemes. Imposing a 120-day suspension regardless of the Eligible 
Facility’s or load’s fault, will not make loads or Eligible Customers any more diligent. In fact, 
given the increased risk and uncertainty, loads that are otherwise willing and able to limit their 
withdrawals could be deterred from applying for the new transmission services and, instead, elect 
NITS, leading to “unnecessary transmission system buildout.”34 
Nor do the North American Electric Reliability Corporation’s (“NERC”) reliability 
standards require suspension of service when a protection scheme misoperates today. NERC 
reliability standards require that the misoperation be investigated and a corrective action plan 
developed.35 If the Commission believes more should be required to ensure reliability, it can direct 
NERC to evaluate and establish reliability standards through the ordinary statutory process. 
Second, the Commission’s approval of the 120-day suspension is logically inconsistent 
with its finding that PJM’s one-strike proposal for failing to follow a curtailment or load shed 
 
33 See, e.g., Comments of Talen Energy Corp., Docket No. AD24-11-000, Analysis Group Report at 12 n.43 (Oct. 28, 
2024) (describing wait times to plan, design, site and construct a new grid connection to be as long as seven years 
for Dominion and seven to ten years for AEP). 
34 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 579. 
35 See Reliability Standard PRC-004-6, Protection System Misoperation and Identification, at R1 (“Each Transmission 
Owner, Generator Owner, and Distribution Provider that owns a BES interrupting device that operated under the 
circumstances in Parts 1.1 through 1.3 shall, within 120 calendar days of the BES interrupting device operation, 
identify whether its Protection System component(s) caused a Misoperation ….”); id. at R5 (“Each Transmission 
Owner, Generator Owner, and Distribution Provider that owns the Protection System component(s) that caused the 
Misoperation shall, within 60 calendar days of first identifying a cause of the Misoperation: … Develop a Corrective 
Action Plan (CAP) for the identified Protection System component(s), and an evaluation of the CAP’s applicability 
to the entity’s other Protection Systems including other locations” or “Explain in a declaration why corrective actions 
are beyond the entity’s control or would not improve BES reliability, and that no further corrective actions will be 
taken.”).

12 
directive is “unnecessarily strict.”36 A four-month loss of transmission service—that has the 
potential to be economically ruinous—effectively amounts to a one-strike proposal.37 If 
disqualification after the first failure to follow a load shed or curtailment directive is “unnecessarily 
strict,” so too should a four-month disqualification for the misoperation of control technologies 
and/or protection systems that may be unrelated to actions taken by the load or Eligible Customer. 
Third, the Commission’s finding failed to consider arguments Constellation raised in its 
May 11 Answer.38 Our May 11 Answer explained that PJM’s claim its 120-day suspension was 
“consistent” with NERC requirements was incorrect, stating, “[t]he NERC Reliability Standards 
that PJM cites—PRC-004-6 (Protection System Misoperation Identification and Correction) and 
PRC-012-2 (Remedial Action Schemes)—set forth a process for investigating whether protection 
systems misoperated and for developing a Corrective Action Plan if appropriate” but neither 
reliability standard “call[ed] for suspension or disqualification of service while an investigation is 
ongoing.”39 While the Commission summarizes our comments,40 the Commission does not 
provide a substantive response.41 Failure to respond to comments raised is an APA violation.42 
 
36 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 515; see also State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43 (“Normally, an 
agency rule would be arbitrary and capricious if the agency … offered an explanation for its decision that runs 
counter to the evidence before the agency ….”). 
37 Depending on the nature of the load, such a loss of service could have ramifications beyond just economic impacts 
for the owner. For example, if the load is a data center running critical national security, banking, medical, 
educational or similar critical applications, the impact may be far broader than just to the owner of the load. 
38 Motion for Leave and Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (May 11, 2026) (“May 11 Answer”). 
39 Id. at 9-10. 
40 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 514. 
41 See id. PP 523-24. 
42 See NEPGA, 881 F.3d at 211 (finding “that FERC did not engage in the reasoned decisionmaking required by the 
Administrative Procedure Act” because it “failed to respond to the substantial arguments put forward by Petitioners 
and failed to square its decision with its past precedent”) (emphasis added); see also State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43 
(“[T]he agency must examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action”).

13 
If the Commission denies our request for rehearing, the Commission should clarify that an 
Eligible Customer could still take transmission service on behalf of other loads during the 
suspension period. This change is necessary to make the suspension and disqualification provisions 
consistent. The June 2026 Co-Location Order found it not just and reasonable to “disqualify the 
Eligible Customer as a whole from taking the relevant transmission service” after the two strikes 
and directed PJM to revise its Tariff to allow the Eligible Customer to “still take transmission 
service, including Interim NITS, FCD transmission service, and NFCD transmission service, on 
behalf of other loads through other transmission service agreements.”43 The same should apply to 
the suspension period if the penalty is not removed. 
IV. 
Transmission Owners Should Not Have Unfettered Discretion over Necessary Control 
Technology Configurations and Resumption of Service After a Misoperation. 
Two findings in the June 2026 Co-Location Order are arbitrary and capricious because they 
grant Transmission Owners unfettered discretion over necessary control technologies and 
protection systems without addressing comments that cautioned against such unchecked 
authority.44 First, the Commission finds that “it is reasonable” that service may resume after the 
suspension “following PJM’s approval, as well as the relevant transmission owner’s approval of 
the necessary control technologies and/or protection systems for consistency with the transmission 
owner’s technical standards.”45 Second, the Commission states, “the transmission owners shall 
 
43 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 527. 
44 See Constellation Apr. 24 Response Brief at 10 (“The Commission should also act to mitigate the Transmission 
Owners’ new proposals that could give them unfettered discretion over the timelines and technical requirements, 
including the following Transmission Owner requests: … ‘[T]he relevant Transmission Owner’s approval must be 
included in the process of allowing service to be reinstated’ after service was suspended; ‘[T]echnical requirements 
should also require an Eligible Customer to satisfy any applicable Transmission Owner-imposed technical 
requirements;’ ‘PJM Transmission Owners request that PJM add, as a condition precedent for receiving service, that 
the Eligible Customer satisfy any load-connection related requirements imposed by the applicable PJM 
Transmission Owner(s);’….”) (emphasis and citations omitted). 
45 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 524 (emphasis added).

14 
have the option to review and agree to the implementation of the Eligible Customer’s necessary 
control technologies and/or protection systems as defined in the service agreement.”46 
While it may be reasonable for Transmission Owners to review necessary control 
technologies and/or protection systems, that review should be bound by Good Utility Practice and 
clear deadlines. Simply stated, Transmission Owners do not favor Co-located Load arrangements 
and have delayed their implementation when given the opportunity to do so.47 As a result, 
Transmission Owner review of necessary control technologies and/or protections systems should 
be consistent with Good Utility Practice, consent should not be unreasonably withheld, and 
Transmission Owner review should be completed within a reasonable time frame (no longer than 
30-60 days). 
As Constellation previously recommended, the Commission should direct PJM to establish 
deadlines for Transmission Owner approvals or consultation requirements and require PJM’s and 
Transmission Owners’ standards, requirements, guidance, and practices on necessary control 
technologies and protection schemes for Co-Location Arrangements to be on file with the 
Commission on a standalone basis or reflected in PJM’s Tariff.48 Rules for Co-Location 
Arrangements must be clearly stated and available as they determine the necessary control 
technologies and protection systems which are a prerequisite to obtaining the new services and 
therefore “significantly affect rates, terms, and conditions” of service and can be “readily 
 
46 Id. P 487 (emphasis added).

susceptible to specification.”49 They cannot be hidden and subject to unilateral change without any

CLARIFICATION 
I. 
The Commission Should Direct PJM to Revise the Definition of Co-Located Generating 
Facility to Conform to the December 2025 Co-Location Order. 
We seek clarification on the Commission’s denial51 of Constellation’s request to revise 
PJM’s definition of Co-Located Generating Facility to “mean the portion of an existing or planned 
Generating Facility that the Interconnection Customer designates to serve and is physically 
connected to a Co-Located Load.”52 Constellation proposed this revision to conform the definition 
of Co-Located Generating Facility with the December 2025 Co-Location Order that specifically 
contemplated a “portion of the generating facility [will] be designated to serve any Co-Located 
Load that is not receiving NITS.”53 No party opposed. Based on these facts, it is unclear why the 
Commission disagreed. The Commission should direct PJM to revise its definition on compliance. 
A more precise definition in the PJM Tariff is critical to reduce uncertainty and potential 
litigation, expedite the interconnection of large loads, and ensure the intent of the December 2025 
Co-Location Order is achieved. Without adding a modifier to “Generating Facility,” some could 
interpret Co-Located Generating Facility as including the entire capacity at a generation site even 
if only a portion of the capacity is contracted to serve the Co-Located Load. For example, where a 
500-MW unit serves a 100-MW Co-Located Load, some could consider the entire 500 MW facility

51 June 2026 Co-Location Order, 195 FERC ¶ 61,209 at P 312. 
52 Constellation 60-Day Compliance Filing Comments at 17 (emphasis in original).  
53 Id. (quoting December 2025 Co-Location Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 230).

16 
as the Generating Facility and thus the Co-Located Generating Facility. This is because PJM 
defines “Generating Facility” as meaning a “Project Developer’s device for the production and/or 
storage for later injection of electricity” which “consists of one or more generating unit(s) and/or 
storage device(s).”54 It is unclear how the June 2026 Co-Location Order’s reference to Part IX, 
Subpart A Form of Application and Studies Agreement, section 2 resolves our concern.55 
Moreover, including the entire capacity of a Generating Facility into a Co-Located 
Generating Facility has real and substantive consequences.56 The Commission found that existing 
generators that are Co-Located Generating Facilities must delist their Capacity Interconnection 
Rights when serving a non-network Co-Located Load.57 The Commission should clarify that a 
hypothetical 500-MW unit serving a 100-MW Co-Located Load via contract demand service is 
not required to delist the entire 500 MW when the load is only 100 MW. Such a requirement would 
needlessly take megawatts out of the system and reduce the capacity available for existing PJM 
customers. 
If the Commission does not grant our clarification, we request rehearing for the 
Commission’s failure to engage in reasoned decision making for failing to provide a rational 
response to the comments raised. 
II. 
An Applicant with a Pending NITS Application Should Be Allowed to Request Interim 
NITS Without Restarting the NITS Process. 
Constellation proposed a transitional mechanism that would allow NITS applicants with 
pending applications to also be deemed to have applied for Interim NITS. The Commission stated

that this is “unnecessary” because “PJM’s proposal does not prohibit any NITS applicant from 
also applying for Interim NITS.”58 That is not responsive to Constellation’s point. To be sure, 
Constellation agrees that an applicant with a pending NITS application should be allowed to apply 
for Interim NITS.59 But Constellation’s concern relates to pending NITS applications. Applicants 
with NITS applications already on file should not be required to go to the back of the line if they 
wish to apply for Interim NITS service as well. 
Accordingly, Constellation requests that the Commission direct PJM to clarify that an 
Interim NITS request can be added to a pending NITS application without causing the applicant 
to restart or delay the NITS process. After all, PJM “designed the new Interim NITS to basically 
be treated the same as regular, full NITS.”60 In this respect, the process for any pending NITS 
request would have been nearly identical had the initial request been for Interim NITS service. In 
addition, in some service territories, NITS applicants have been waiting nearly a decade to be 
interconnected to the grid.61 These applicants should not have to wait any longer for service. If 
these applicants will be forced to the “back of the line” for requesting Interim NITS, most are 
unlikely to do so even though they may be willing and able to limit their energy withdrawals. The 
Commission and PJM will have unnecessarily reduced the pool of large loads that are “critical to

CONCLUSION 
For the reasons set forth above, Constellation respectfully requests that the Commission 
grant rehearing and clarification of the June 2026 Co-Location Order.
